text.p: Cuba published a document on Saturday calling for the defence of its one-party socialist system and said discussion of the paper would represent a "new plebiscite for the Cuban people" on the revolution.

The document, which will be a focal point in the Oct. 8-10 Fifth Party Congress, was formally published by the ruling Communist Party daily Granma. It is due to be debated across the island of 11 million people from June 1 to July 15.
Granma said the nation was "on the eve of what will be a new plebiscite of our heroic people for the Nation, the Revolution and Socialism".
"Once more, dignity, reason, conscience and patriotism will predominate and will win," the newspaper said.
It argued there was no lack of democracy in Cuba when the masses "discuss openly and frankly a document of this dimension".

The eight-page party document makes plain that at least at leadership level, President Fidel Castro's party is not planning any major political changes at the October congress, which will map strategy for the party and country into the year 2000 and beyond.
There has been no indication yet as to how far ordinary Cubans will be able to suggest or make changes to the document.
But Cuba's system means it is often not easy for people to express disagreement with the official line in organised gatherings, although they may grumble in their homes or among friends.
Granma itself indicated what was expected of citizens, saying the debate would spark wide reflections on "patriotic, revolutionary and socialist convictions."

The document calls on Cubans to back the socialist system as the only means of preserving the island's independence. It draws heavily on history to argue there is no alternative for the country, urging Cubans to unite against what is portrayed as a greater than ever threat from the United States.
Washington's pressure for change in Cuba, a constant since the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power, is always presented by Havana as an effort to erode the island's independence.
Granma's comment on Saturday stressed the breadth of the forthcoming debate, noting it will involve some 770,000 Communist Party members and nearly half a million Union of Youth Communists members.
Discussion will also be organised by 80,000 labour union branches, 120,000 neighbourhood committees, 76,000 women's union branches, 4,000 workers' cooperatives and 20,000 student union branches.

The newspaper gave as an example of people's overwhelming support for the "revolution, the party and its historical leadership" the recent signature by some eight million people of a declaration rejecting a White House document outlining international aid Cuba might receive if it embarked on a transition. People were urged to sign the declaration across the country.

The October party congress will be the first since October 1991, when Cuba was on the brink of severe economic crisis triggered by the demise of its old economic and political ally the former Soviet Union.
Cuba undertook some cautious economic reforms from 1993 onward. But Castro, 70, has made increasingly clear he does not view the island as on the road to capitalism.
